**The Art of Wandering: A Love Letter to the Unplanned**

There’s a certain magic in not knowing where you’re going. Not in the sense of being lost, but in the sense of allowing the world to unfold before you, unscripted, unfiltered. Life, when stripped of rigid itineraries and over-planned days, becomes a series of small, unexpected miracles—like stumbling upon a café in Lisbon where the espresso tastes like liquid gold, or getting lost in a Parisian bookstore that smells of old paper and distant dreams. The best things in life, I’ve found, are rarely the ones we chase with precision. They’re the ones that find us when we’re not looking.

I’ve always been a planner. Not in the way that suggests control or rigidity, but in the way that suggests a deep, almost compulsive need to *know*—to map out the future, to anticipate every possible outcome, to leave nothing to chance. For years, I carried a bullet journal, color-coded my calendar, and made spreadsheets for everything from grocery lists to potential career moves. I was the kind of person who would research a restaurant’s menu before even stepping inside, who would memorize the train schedule in a foreign city before booking the ticket. There was comfort in knowing. In having a plan.

But then, one day, I realized something: the best moments of my life had happened *outside* the plan.

It was a rainy afternoon in Kyoto, and I had spent the morning meticulously planning my route to the Fushimi Inari Shrine. I had read about the thousands of torii gates, the winding paths up the mountain, the way the vermilion gates would glow in the sunlight. I had even downloaded an offline map. But when I arrived, the sky was a heavy gray, the kind that makes the world feel soft and muted. The gates were still there, of course—thousands of them, stretching up the hill like a river of red—but they weren’t glowing. They were quiet. Mysterious. And as I walked, the rain began to fall, just a light mist at first, then a steady drizzle. I had brought an umbrella, but I didn’t open it. Instead, I let the rain touch my face, let the mist settle on my skin.

And then I heard it—the sound of a shamisen, a traditional Japanese stringed instrument, drifting from somewhere up the hill. I followed the music, slipping past the tourists who were huddled under their umbrellas, and found a small shrine where an elderly man was playing. He didn’t stop when he saw me. He just nodded and kept playing, his fingers moving deftly over the strings. I stood there for what felt like an hour, listening, watching the rain blur the edges of the world. When I finally left, I didn’t have a single photo of the shrine. I didn’t even have a clear memory of the path I took to get there. But I had something better: the memory of a moment that felt like a secret, something only I had witnessed.

That’s when I started to question the tyranny of the plan.

---

There’s a Japanese concept called *komorebi* (木漏れ日), which refers to the way sunlight filters through the leaves of trees. It’s a word that captures the beauty of something fleeting, something that can’t be controlled or replicated. Life, in many ways, is like *komorebi*—a series of dappled, shifting moments that only exist in the present. And yet, how often do we rush past them, too busy chasing the next thing on our list to notice the light filtering through the trees?

I think about all the times I’ve missed the *komorebi* in my own life. The times I was so focused on the destination that I forgot to enjoy the journey. The times I was so worried about what might happen that I didn’t stop to appreciate what *was* happening. There’s a quote I love by John Lennon: *"Life is what happens to you while you're busy making other plans."* And it’s true. Life isn’t a straight line from point A to point B. It’s a meandering path, full of detours and dead ends and unexpected turns. The best things—the things that linger in your memory long after the facts have faded—are the ones that happen when you’re not looking.

I’ve been thinking a lot lately about the idea of *serendipity*—those beautiful, unplanned moments that feel like gifts. The kind of moments that can’t be forced, only surrendered to. Like the time I got on a train in Italy without a destination, just because the conductor’s accent was charming and the seats were empty. I ended up in a tiny village in Tuscany where an old woman fed me fresh figs and homemade wine, and I didn’t speak a word of Italian. Or the time I took a wrong turn in Marrakech and stumbled into a courtyard where a group of women were preparing a feast, and they insisted I stay for dinner, even though I could barely communicate with them.

These are the moments that define us, not the ones we plan. They’re the ones that remind us that we’re alive, that the world is vast and mysterious and full of wonder. They’re the ones that make life feel like an adventure, not a checklist.

---

I’ve been trying, lately, to embrace the art of wandering. Not the kind of wandering that comes from being lost, but the kind that comes from choosing not to know. The kind that says, *"I don’t have to have it all figured out. I can just be here, in this moment, and see where it takes me."*

It’s not always easy. There’s a certain anxiety that comes with not having a plan. What if I miss my train? What if I get lost? What if something goes wrong? But then I remember that the things that go wrong are often the things that lead to the best stories. The missed train that leads to a spontaneous conversation with a stranger who becomes a lifelong friend. The wrong turn that leads to a hidden café where the barista knows your name. The detour that leads to a sunset so beautiful it makes your chest ache.

There’s a freedom in surrendering to the unknown. A freedom in trusting that, even if you don’t have a plan, the world will unfold in a way that’s meant for you. It’s not about being reckless or irresponsible. It’s about being open. About saying yes to the things that don’t fit neatly into your schedule. About allowing yourself to be surprised.

I’ve started to keep a *"wandering journal"*—not a detailed itinerary, but a place to jot down the things that catch my eye. A sketch of a building that looks like it’s straight out of a fairy tale. A conversation with a stranger about the meaning of life. The way the light hits a street at a certain time of day. It’s not about documenting every moment, but about noticing the ones that matter.

---

I think about the people who inspire me—the ones who live their lives with a sense of adventure, who say yes to the things that scare them, who embrace the unknown with open arms. Like the woman I met in Peru who quit her corporate job to hike the Inca Trail with nothing but a backpack and a dream. Or the man in India who left his job to travel the country in a rickshaw, documenting the stories of the people he met along the way. Or the couple who sold everything they owned to sail around the world, just because they could.

These are people who understand that life isn’t about accumulating things or checking boxes. It’s about collecting experiences, about letting the world surprise you, about trusting that even when things don’t go according to plan, they’re still going somewhere good.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the idea of *"beginner’s mind"*—a concept from Zen Buddhism that refers to approaching life with curiosity and openness, as if you’re seeing everything for the first time. It’s the opposite of the planner’s mind, which is always looking ahead, always trying to control the future. Beginner’s mind is about being present. About saying, *"I don’t know what’s going to happen next, and that’s okay."*

There’s a certain humility in not knowing. A certain grace. It’s the humility of the traveler who realizes that the world is bigger than they are, that there are things they’ll never understand, places they’ll never see, people they’ll never meet. But it’s also the grace of the traveler who understands that they don’t have to understand everything. They just have to be there, in the moment, open to whatever comes next.

---

I’ve been trying to apply this to my own life. Not just in travel, but in everything. In my relationships, in my work, in the way I move through the world. I’m trying to be more present. To listen more deeply. To say yes to the things that don’t fit into my schedule. To embrace the unknown, even when it’s scary.

It’s not always easy. There are days when I slip back into old habits—when I over-plan, when I stress about the future, when I forget to stop and look at the light filtering through the trees. But I’m learning. Slowly, imperfectly, but I’m learning.

And I think that’s the key. Not to be perfect. Not to have it all figured out. But to keep trying. To keep wandering. To keep saying yes to the unknown.

Because life, after all, isn’t about the destination. It’s about the journey. And the best journeys are the ones that don’t have a map.

---

So here’s to the unplanned. To the detours and the dead ends and the unexpected turns. To the moments that can’t be forced, only surrendered to. To the light filtering through the leaves, to the music drifting up the hill, to the strangers who become friends, to the places that feel like home even when you’ve never been there before.

Here’s to the art of wandering. May we all get a little lost sometimes.
